q: The general formula of saturated monocarboxylic acids is:
x: An alkyl group CₙH₂ₙ₊₁ joined to –COOH gives the series HCOOH (n = 0), CH₃COOH, C₂H₅COOH and so on. –CHO belongs to aldehydes.

q: A chlorine atom is attached to the carbon farthest from the carboxyl group in ClCH₂CH₂COOH. Its systematic name is:
x: Numbering starts at the carboxyl carbon (C-1), so the chlorine is on C-3 of a three-carbon acid.

q: Oxalic acid, HOOC–COOH, has the IUPAC name:
x: It has two carbons, both in –COOH groups, so it is ethanedioic acid. Ethanoic acid has only one carboxyl group.

q: Which type of alcohol can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms?
x: Primary alcohols are oxidised first to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids. Secondary alcohols give ketones, and tertiary alcohols resist oxidation.

q: Methylbenzene (toluene) is heated with alkaline KMnO₄ and then acidified. The organic product is:
x: Strong oxidation converts the side-chain –CH₃ on a benzene ring into –COOH, giving C₆H₅COOH.

q: Ethanoic acid mixes with water in all proportions mainly because:
o: Its –COOH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules
It has a very high molar mass
It reacts completely with water to form ethanol
x: The C=O and O–H of the carboxyl group hydrogen-bond with water, so lower acids are miscible; solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain grows.

q: Pure ethanoic acid is called glacial acetic acid because:
o: It freezes into ice-like crystals at about 17 °C
It is a colourless gas at room temperature
x: Pure ethanoic acid has a freezing point of about 16.6 °C, so in cold weather it solidifies into an ice-like mass.

q: Which Grignard reagent, after reaction with carbon dioxide and hydrolysis with dilute acid, gives propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH?
x: The CO₂ adds one carbon as –COOH, so a two-carbon (ethyl) Grignard gives the three-carbon acid. CH₃MgBr would give ethanoic acid.

q: Ethanoic acid ionises in water: CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺. The conjugate base of ethanoic acid is:
x: Removing H⁺ from CH₃COOH gives CH₃COO⁻, its conjugate base. H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of water.

q: Ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium ribbon. The products are:
x: Like other acids, it reacts with a reactive metal: 2CH₃COOH + Mg → (CH₃COO)₂Mg + H₂.

q: Fluoroethanoic acid, FCH₂COOH, is a stronger acid than chloroethanoic acid, ClCH₂COOH, because:
o: Fluorine is more electronegative and has a stronger electron-withdrawing inductive effect
Fluorine releases electrons towards the carboxyl group
The C–F bond breaks more easily than the C–Cl bond
x: The stronger −I effect of fluorine pulls more electron density from the carboxylate ion, stabilising it and making H⁺ loss easier.

q: Anhydrous sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime (NaOH and CaO). The gas formed is:
x: This is decarboxylation: CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃. The –COO group leaves as carbonate, so the product has one carbon fewer.

q: 3.0 g of ethanoic acid (Mr 60) is added to excess sodium carbonate: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + CO₂ + H₂O. What volume of CO₂ is formed at STP? (1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: Moles of acid = 3.0/60 = 0.05; CO₂ = 0.05/2 = 0.025 mol; 0.025 × 22.4 = 0.56 dm³. Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio gives 1.12 dm³.

q: Ethanoic acid is treated with chlorine in the presence of red phosphorus. The main organic product is:
x: Chlorine replaces an α-hydrogen (on the carbon next to –COOH) to give ClCH₂COOH. Ethanoyl chloride is made with SOCl₂ or PCl₅, not Cl₂.

q: 2-chlorobutanoic acid is a stronger acid than 4-chlorobutanoic acid. The reason is that:
o: Chlorine releases electrons when it is close to the –COOH group
The inductive effect of chlorine weakens with distance, so it stabilises the anion more when closer to –COOH
2-chlorobutanoic acid forms hydrogen bonds but 4-chlorobutanoic acid cannot
x: Both have the same formula; the −I effect falls off quickly along the chain, so chlorine on C-2 withdraws electrons from the carboxylate far more than on C-4.

q: The ester CH₃COOCH₃ is named:
x: The alkyl group from the alcohol (methyl) is named first, then the acid part (ethanoate, from CH₃COO–).

q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol at room temperature. The products are:
x: CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl. Unlike esterification of the acid, this reaction is fast and goes to completion.

q: Ethanoic anhydride can be made by heating ethanoic acid with phosphorus pentoxide, P₂O₅. The role of P₂O₅ is to act as a:
o: Dehydrating agent, removing a water molecule from two acid molecules
x: 2CH₃COOH → (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O; P₂O₅ removes the water, joining two acid molecules into the anhydride.

q: Ethanoic anhydride, (CH₃CO)₂O, is hydrolysed by water. The product is:
x: (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O → 2CH₃COOH: adding water reverses the dehydration that formed the anhydride.

q: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is boiled with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The products are:
x: Alkaline hydrolysis of an amide gives the carboxylate salt and ammonia gas: CH₃CONH₂ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + NH₃.

q: Which carboxylic acid and alcohol react together to form the ester CH₃CH₂COOCH₃?
x: The acyl part CH₃CH₂CO– comes from propanoic acid and –OCH₃ from methanol. Ethanoic acid with ethanol gives an isomer, ethyl ethanoate.

q: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of an ester is reversible, but hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH goes to completion. The reason is that in alkaline hydrolysis:
o: NaOH is a stronger catalyst than H⁺
The acid formed is converted to its carboxylate ion, which does not react with the alcohol
The ester is converted into an amide
x: The carboxylate anion cannot be attacked by the alcohol to re-form the ester, so the back reaction is removed and hydrolysis is complete.
